topic: a city council's decision to replace a public park with affordable housing
wrong_topic: a review of a new restaurant opening downtown
text: Last Tuesday the council voted six to three to rezone Linden Park. The fourteen-acre green space, home to a community garden and two aging baseball diamonds, will give way to roughly four hundred apartments, at least half of them priced below market rate. Supporters packed the chamber with signs reading "Homes, Not Hedges." They pointed out that the median rent in the city has risen forty percent in five years and that the waiting list for subsidized units now exceeds eleven thousand households. Opponents, many of them longtime residents of the surrounding blocks, argued that the park is the only open space within walking distance for thousands of children, and that the council ignored two vacant parking lots owned by the city just a mile away. The mayor, who had promised during her campaign to protect green space, abstained. A spokesperson for the developer said construction could begin within eighteen months, pending an environmental review. Several residents have already announced plans to file a lawsuit, claiming that the public notice for the hearing was posted only on the city website and never mailed to nearby households. The council member who introduced the measure called the lawsuit a delaying tactic and said that every month of delay means more families leaving the city. Whether the decision represents courage or betrayal seems to depend largely on which side of the park fence one lives on.

topic: a company's new policy of monitoring remote employees' keystrokes
wrong_topic: a scientific study about sleep and memory
text: Starting next month, every remote employee at Brightline Logistics will install software that records keystrokes, active application time, and a screenshot every ten minutes. The company's chief operating officer described the change in an internal memo as a step toward "fairness and transparency," noting that some teams had complained about colleagues who appeared to be online but delivered little. The memo promised that the data would be used only in aggregate and never for individual discipline without a manager's review. Employees reacted quickly. Within hours, an anonymous survey circulated on a workplace forum, and more than seventy percent of respondents said they would consider leaving. Some argued that productivity should be judged by results, not by mouse movements. Others quietly admitted that they had seen coworkers exploit the flexibility of remote work and were not entirely opposed. A labor lawyer consulted by a local newspaper said the policy is legal in most states as long as employees are informed in writing. The company's quarterly earnings, released the same week, showed a modest decline in margins, which some employees believe is the real motivation. Management has not responded to requests for comment on that point. For now, the software rollout remains on schedule, and the memo ends with a line that has been quoted widely: "Trust is built when everyone can see the same picture."

topic: a student athlete being disqualified after a positive test for a cold medicine
wrong_topic: the history of medieval trade routes
text: Mara Okafor had trained for four years for the regional championship. She won the 800 meters by nearly two seconds, the fastest time in the state this season. Three days later, the athletic association announced that her result had been voided. A routine test had detected a stimulant found in a common over-the-counter cold medicine, which she says she took the night before the race because of a sore throat. Her coach insists that no one ever told the team that the medicine was on the banned list, and that the list itself is a forty-page document written in technical language. The association responded that every athlete signs a form acknowledging responsibility for anything they ingest, and that the rule exists precisely because intent is impossible to prove. The runner-up, who now holds the title, said in a brief statement that she felt sorry for Okafor but believed the rules must apply to everyone equally. A petition asking for the decision to be reversed has collected over twenty thousand signatures. Some former athletes have signed it; others have publicly warned that making exceptions would open the door to abuse. Okafor's scholarship offer from a university is now under review. She has not raced since, and her family says she rarely leaves the house.

topic: a town debating whether to remove a statue of its founder
text: The bronze statue of Elias Harrow has stood in front of the town library since 1911. Harrow founded the town, donated the land for its first school, and paid for the library itself. He also, according to records uncovered last year by a graduate student, made much of his fortune by evicting tenant farmers during a drought and buying their land at a fraction of its value. Since the records were published, the statue has been splashed with red paint twice. At a crowded public meeting, a retired teacher said that removing the statue would erase the town's history and that every historical figure had flaws. A young organizer replied that a statue is not history but honor, and that history would remain in the books and the archive. Several speakers proposed a compromise: keep the statue but add a plaque describing the evictions. Others objected that a plaque would be easy to ignore. The library board, which technically owns the statue, has said it will follow the result of a nonbinding vote scheduled for the spring. Descendants of both Harrow and the evicted families still live in town, and some of them attend the same church. One of them told a reporter that she was tired of being asked which side she was on.

topic: a hospital rationing a scarce drug using a lottery
wrong_topic: a travel guide to coastal beaches
text: When the shortage began, the hospital had enough of the drug for roughly one in three eligible patients. The ethics committee met for two days. In the end, they chose a lottery: every patient who met the medical criteria would be entered, and a computer would select who received treatment each week. The committee chair explained that any other method, such as prioritizing younger patients or those with better prognoses, would require doctors to make judgments about whose life mattered more. Some families accepted the decision with resignation. Others were furious. A man whose mother was not selected said it felt like gambling with lives, and asked why the hospital had not prioritized the sickest patients first. A physician on the committee responded that the sickest patients were often the least likely to benefit, and that choosing them would mean fewer lives saved overall. A local politician demanded an investigation, while a national bioethics group praised the hospital for its transparency. Meanwhile, the manufacturer has said that new supply will not arrive for at least four months. Nurses report that the weekly announcement of results has become the hardest hour of their shift. The committee has agreed to revisit the policy monthly, but no one has proposed an alternative that the members find clearly fairer.
